title: You're On Your Own, Kid
description: Track five on Midnights, and a full life story in three minutes — Swift races from sprinkler splashes to fireplace ashes, growing up verse by verse until independence stops sounding lonely and starts sounding earned.

pops.text: It's the fifth track on Midnights (2022) — and longtime fans know track five is sacred ground for Swift, traditionally reserved for an album's most exposed, emotional song.
Swift wrote and produced it with Jack Antonoff, her chief Midnights collaborator; the two built most of the album together in late-night studio sessions.
She unveiled the title in her TikTok series Midnights Mayhem With Me, pulling numbered ping-pong balls from a bingo cage to reveal one track at a time.
There is no narrative music video — the official upload is the lyric video released with the album on October 21, 2022.
The lyric 'make the friendship bracelets' escaped the song entirely: trading handmade bracelets became the defining fan ritual of the Eras Tour.
When Midnights landed, Swift became the first artist ever to occupy the entire Billboard Hot 100 top ten at once — and this song was one of those ten.
The bridge name-checks a 'Daisy Mae,' which sent fans sleuthing for clues about the children of Swift's famous friends.
Structurally it's a sprint through a whole biography: childhood summers, a first crush, moving away, and learning that nobody is coming to do it for you.
Critics singled it out as Midnights' autobiographical peak — less a breakup song than a report card on fame, friendship and growing up in public.
On the Eras Tour it became a beloved live moment, with tens of thousands of friendship-braceleted fans singing the bridge back at her.

title: Bang and Blame
description: The second single from Monster, R.E.M.'s loud, glammy 1994 reset — a trembling guitar, a relationship gone wrong, and Michael Stipe coolly itemizing exactly whose fault everything is.

pops.text: Monster (1994) was a deliberate swerve: after two quiet, acoustic-leaning albums, R.E.M. plugged back in and made the loud rock record fans kept asking for.
Released as Monster's second single, it climbed to No. 19 on the Billboard Hot 100 — a strong showing for such a spiky song.
It topped Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks chart, becoming one of the band's defining alternative-radio hits of the decade.
The official video is stark black-and-white, matching the song's accusatory, no-place-to-hide mood.
Peter Buck's guitar shimmers with tremolo throughout — the wobbling tone is the sound of Monster's glam-rock experiment in miniature.
Monster debuted at No. 1 in both the US and the UK, the commercial peak of R.E.M.'s arena years.
Another Monster track, 'Let Me In,' was written in response to the death of Kurt Cobain, a friend of Michael Stipe's — grief runs under the album's noise.
The Monster tour was drummer Bill Berry's last full campaign with the band; he suffered a brain aneurysm on stage in Switzerland in 1995 and left R.E.M. in 1997.
Berry, Buck, Mills and Stipe share the writing credit — still the original four-man lineup, three albums into their major-label era.
Monster's liner notes and garish orange artwork nodded to glam and trash culture — the whole era was R.E.M. in smeared eyeliner, having fun with fame.

title: Jumpin' Jack Flash
description: A stand-alone 1968 single that rebooted the Stones: Keith Richards' overloaded cassette-recorder riff, Mick Jagger howling about being born in a crossfire hurricane, and blues-rock perfection in three and a half minutes.

pops.text: It was released in 1968 as a stand-alone single, not on any studio album — and it shot to No. 1 in the UK and No. 3 in the US.
Keith Richards has said 'Jack' was his gardener, Jack Dyer; Jagger, woken one night by Dyer's boots squelching past, asked about the noise and Richards answered, 'Jumpin' Jack.'
The 'Flash' arrived as Jagger improvised around the phrase — the gardener got a co-starring role in rock history without ever picking up an instrument.
That gritty guitar crunch? Richards recorded an acoustic guitar into an overloaded Philips cassette recorder, then used the distorted cassette sound as the track's foundation.
Bassist Bill Wyman long maintained he dreamed up the central riff on an organ during a studio jam — a contribution he felt was never properly credited.
The song marked the Stones' return to hard blues-rock after the psychedelic detour of Their Satanic Majesties Request, setting up the Beggars Banquet era.
Two promo films were shot in a single day at Olympic Studios in London, directed by Michael Lindsay-Hogg — one with the band in wild makeup, one without.
Both versions were restored in 4K and officially re-released in 2022, more than fifty years after they were filmed.
Nicky Hopkins supplies the rolling piano that tumbles through the track behind the riff.
It became a permanent fixture of Stones concerts — one of the most-performed songs in the band's entire live history.

title: Pilgrims
description: A slow-building travelogue from Everyday, the Athens band's third album: black cats, crows and weary wanderers, resolving into John Bell's simple road philosophy — if it feels good, we shake.

pops.text: 'Pilgrims' comes from Everyday (1993), Widespread Panic's third studio album, where it runs a full six and a half minutes.
Everyday was recorded at Muscle Shoals Sound Studio in Sheffield, Alabama — hallowed ground for Southern soul and rock recording.
Producer Johnny Sandlin, a Capricorn Records veteran, helmed the sessions and gave the band's live sprawl a studio frame.
It was the group's first album with keyboardist John 'JoJo' Hermann as a full band member — his piano is now part of the band's DNA.
Look closely at the Everyday album cover: the model is a then-unknown Angelina Jolie, years before film stardom.
Everyday was a slow burn commercially, peaking at No. 184 on the Billboard 200 while the band built its reputation on the road instead.
Singer-guitarist John Bell delivers the vocal in his trademark gravelly drawl, half preacher and half fellow traveler.
The lyric opens with a black cat crossing the path 'on little fog feet' — a nod to Carl Sandburg's famous fog poem, filtered through Southern superstition.
Its chorus boils the band's whole ethos down to one line: 'Listen — if it feels good, we shake.'
Decades on, 'Pilgrims' remains a setlist cornerstone, regularly opening or anchoring Panic shows on their endless touring circuit.

title: Cumberland Blues
description: A breakneck bluegrass sprint from Workingman's Dead: a Cumberland coal miner who can't quit the mine that owns him, sung in tight harmonies by a band reinventing itself as an American roots group.

pops.text: It opens the second side of Workingman's Dead (1970), the album where the Grateful Dead traded psychedelic sprawl for tight, harmony-driven Americana.
The writing is credited to Jerry Garcia, Phil Lesh and lyricist Robert Hunter — a rare three-way credit in the Dead catalog.
The band first played it live on November 8, 1969, at the Fillmore West in San Francisco, months before the album appeared.
Workingman's Dead was cut quickly — the band recorded the album in roughly nine days at Pacific High Recording in San Francisco.
The close harmonies were a new trick: the Dead had been absorbing Crosby, Stills & Nash's vocal blend and set out to build songs around singing, not just jamming.
The narrator is trapped in the classic company-town bind — he owes his soul to the mine, makes money, and still can't go home 'thisaway.'
It's one of the fastest things on the record, a bluegrass gallop with Garcia's guitar darting between the vocal lines.
A celebrated live version anchors the Europe '72 tour recordings, where the song regularly stretched its legs.
The official audio here is the 2020 remaster, issued for the album's 50th anniversary deluxe edition.
Workingman's Dead later went platinum in the US — the 'stripped-down' album became one of the Dead's best-selling studio records.

title: Cry Me a River
description: Krall live at the Paris Olympia, turning Arthur Hamilton's torch standard into a slow-burning dare: Claus Ogerman's orchestral glow behind her, and a lover who cried once too often getting told to return the favour.

pops.text: Arthur Hamilton published this torch song in 1953 — he first wrote it for Ella Fitzgerald to sing in the film Pete Kelly's Blues, but her number was cut.
Julie London made it famous in 1955. Hamilton had been her high-school classmate, and her million-selling version was backed by just guitar and bass.
London's recording reached No. 9 in the US, she sang it on screen in The Girl Can't Help It (1956), and it was later inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.
Krall first recorded the song in the studio for The Look of Love (2001), where it sits as track four under Claus Ogerman's lush orchestral arrangements.
This performance is the live one: Krall filmed Live in Paris at the Olympia Theatre over four nights in late November and early December 2001.
Live in Paris arrived in 2002 as her first live album — and it went on to win the Grammy Award for Best Jazz Vocal Album.
Watch the band hold back: guitarist Anthony Wilson, bassist Christian McBride and drummer Lewis Nash leave Krall's piano and voice all the air they need.
The Live in Paris film gives this song extra room — 'Cry Me a River' appears in the DVD performance footage beyond the album's core track list.
Hundreds of singers have taken on this standard, from Barbra Streisand to Joe Cocker — Krall's edge is how quietly she delivers the payback.
The whole lyric is a reversal: you made me cry, now the river runs the other way. Krall never raises her voice, which makes it colder — and better.

title: Solsbury Hill
description: Gabriel's solo debut single and gentle goodbye to Genesis: an acoustic walk up a Somerset hill at night, an eagle, a voice, and a decision — in lopsided 7/4 time — to let go of the life he had.

pops.text: Released in March 1977, this was Peter Gabriel's first single as a solo artist, taken from his self-titled debut album — the one fans nicknamed Car.
Gabriel had walked away from Genesis in 1975, the progressive band he co-founded in 1967 and fronted in famously elaborate stage costumes.
The hill is real: Little Solsbury Hill in Somerset, near Bath, is an Iron Age hill fort — Gabriel wrote the song after a spiritual experience up there.
He has summed the song up simply: it is about being prepared to lose what you have for what you might get. It is about letting go.
Most of the song moves in 7/4 time — seven beats to the bar instead of the usual four — which gives its easy stride a permanent slight lean forward.
Producer Bob Ezrin shaped the debut album, and the record was made at The Soundstage studios in Toronto; this was the last track recorded for it.
That warm acoustic guitar part belongs to Steve Hunter — King Crimson's Robert Fripp played elsewhere on the album but, by his own account, contributed nothing here.
Listen for the beat: drummer Allan Schwartzberg reportedly got that soft thump by striking a telephone directory with a drumstick, shaker in his other hand.
Gabriel himself adds flute alongside his vocal and keyboards — a pastoral touch left over from the Genesis toolkit, put to much simpler use.
It peaked at No. 13 in the UK and No. 68 on the Billboard Hot 100 — modest numbers for a song that never really left radio, films or Gabriel's live sets.

title: Something
description: George Harrison steps out of the Lennon–McCartney shadow on Abbey Road: a love song with a borrowed first line, Billy Preston's organ, George Martin's strings, and a melody Sinatra could not resist.

pops.text: Harrison wrote it — it is track two on Abbey Road (1969), and together with 'Here Comes the Sun' it announced him as a songwriter of the first rank.
He began it on piano in September 1968, during sessions for the White Album, while Paul McCartney worked on overdubs in the next studio.
The opening line came from James Taylor: 'Something in the Way She Moves' was a song on Taylor's Apple Records debut, recorded down the hall that same autumn.
Harrison demoed it solo on 25 February 1969, his 26th birthday — that spare demo later surfaced on Anthology 3.
When he wrote it, he heard Ray Charles singing it in his head; Charles did eventually record his own version.
It is generally read as a love song to Harrison's wife Pattie Boyd, though in later years he pointed just as happily toward Krishna as its subject.
Billy Preston, the Beatles' favourite guest musician that year, adds the hymn-like organ part under Harrison's vocal.
Released as a double A-side single with 'Come Together' in October 1969, it became Harrison's first Beatles single — and the pairing topped the US chart.
Frank Sinatra called it the greatest love song of the previous fifty years and made it a live staple — though he sometimes introduced it as a Lennon–McCartney song.
By the late 1970s more than 150 artists had covered it, making it the second-most covered Beatles song after 'Yesterday' — Shirley Bassey's version was a UK top-five hit.

title: You're Welcome
description: Maui's two-minute résumé, sung by Dwayne Johnson in Moana: the demigod who lassoed the sun and pulled islands from the sea lists his gifts to humanity — and graciously accepts your thanks in advance.

pops.text: Lin-Manuel Miranda wrote the song for Moana (2016), part of a soundtrack built with composer Mark Mancina and Opetaia Foa'i of Te Vaka.
Johnson voices Maui, the shapeshifting demigod Moana finds on a deserted island — this number is his introduction, and he wastes none of it on modesty.
Miranda did his homework on Johnson's voice by watching old wrestling footage: as a WWE villain, Johnson used to serenade crowds with a guitar to insult them.
The lyric is Maui's greatest-hits reel — tides, sun, sky, islands fished up from the ocean floor — each feat answered with the same smug refrain.
Keep an eye on Maui's tattoos during the film sequence: his miniature ink double, Mini Maui, acts out reactions the big demigod is too cool to show.
Johnson was a blockbuster action star and former wrestler, not a singer — which is exactly why Miranda built the song around patter, rhythm and charm.
A second version with Jordan Fisher singing alongside Miranda plays over the film's end credits, but the movie moment is Johnson's alone.
Moana's soundtrack album, released in November 2016, peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard 200, held off the top only by The Weeknd's Starboy.
Johnson's recording was released as a single in December 2016 and climbed to No. 65 on the Billboard Hot 100 — a chart hit for The Rock, the singer.
The soundtrack went on to spend a record-setting 61 weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's Soundtracks chart — Maui would insist you are welcome for that, too.

title: How Far I'll Go
description: Moana's great 'I want' song, written by Lin-Manuel Miranda and sung by a Hawaiian high-school freshman in her first-ever film role — the sound of a wayfinder hearing the ocean call her name.

pops.text: Lin-Manuel Miranda wrote it for Moana (2016), fresh off the phenomenon of Hamilton.
Cravalho was a high-school freshman from Hawaii when she was cast — this was her first professional acting or singing role.
She nearly didn't audition: convinced stronger singers were trying out, she was discovered when a casting agent spotted her singing in a charity-competition video.
She was the very last person auditioned, on the final day of the search for Moana's voice.
The song is Moana's classic Disney 'I want' moment — the horizon, not a prince, is what she's longing for.
It was nominated for the Academy Award and Golden Globe for Best Original Song.
It won the Grammy Award for Best Song Written for Visual Media.
Cravalho performed it live at the 2017 Oscars, introduced by Miranda, wearing a red gown that matched the ceremony's most replayed performance clip.
Alessia Cara recorded the pop single version heard over the film's end credits — but the movie moment belongs to Cravalho.
At 16, she became one of the youngest voices ever to headline a Disney animated feature — and Moana's call to the sea became a generation's anthem.

title: Breath
description: A Ten-era orphan that found its home on the Singles soundtrack: Stone Gossard's Mother Love Bone-era riff, Eddie Vedder pleading for air, and a fan-favorite anthem the band left off its debut.

pops.text: 'Breath' appeared on the soundtrack to Cameron Crowe's Singles (1992), the definitive document of Seattle's grunge moment.
Stone Gossard wrote the music; Mike McCready has said the song dates back to Gossard's days in Mother Love Bone, before Pearl Jam existed.
Eddie Vedder wrote the lyrics — the whole song is one escalating plea for a moment to breathe.
It was recorded around the Ten sessions but left off the album, which only raised its legend among fans.
The soundtrack album arrived in June 1992, three months before the film — and helped carry grunge fully into the mainstream.
Vedder, Gossard and Jeff Ament appear in Singles as Citizen Dick, the fictional band fronted by Matt Dillon's character.
For years fans held up 'BREATH' signs at concerts, turning setlist requests for it into a running piece of Pearl Jam lore.
The song finally got wider release on the band's 2004 greatest-hits collection, Rearviewmirror.
Crowe was a longtime Seattle ally — he also put Pearl Jam's story at the heart of his documentary Pearl Jam Twenty.
Producer Rick Parashar, who co-produced Ten, worked on the track — the family resemblance to the debut album is no accident.

title: Lawyers, Guns and Money
description: The closing track of Excitable Boy: a rich kid ricochets from Havana to Honduras to Russia, wiring Dad for rescue each time — the funniest three-word emergency plan in rock history.

pops.text: It's the final track on Excitable Boy (1978), Zevon's best-selling album — the emergency call comes after nine songs of werewolves and excitable boys.
Jackson Browne produced the album, part of the Asylum Records circle that championed Zevon through the seventies.
The narrator careens through three verses of international incidents — gambling in Havana, hiding in Honduras, and a fatal misunderstanding involving Russians.
Each chorus is the same telegram home: 'Send lawyers, guns and money — Dad, get me out of this.'
Zevon never released it as a hit single; it became a standard purely through album play, covers and word of mouth.
Hank Williams Jr. covered it and took the song onto the country charts in the late 1980s.
The guitar muscle comes from Waddy Wachtel, Zevon's longtime collaborator, whose stinging leads run all over Excitable Boy.
Zevon was a novelist's songwriter — steeped in crime fiction, his verses read like a Ross Macdonald plot compressed into three minutes.
He became David Letterman's favorite musical guest, filling in as bandleader when Paul Shaffer was away.
Zevon, who died in 2003, was posthumously inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2025 — the rescue party finally arrived.

title: It's All Right
description: Curtis Mayfield's two-minute dose of pure reassurance: born from a bandmate's offhand exclamation in Nashville, it topped the R&B chart, hit No. 4 pop, and bought three young singers their first houses.

pops.text: Curtis Mayfield wrote it after bandmate Fred Cash, talking excitedly about the group's future between shows in Nashville, exclaimed, 'It's all right!'
Released in 1963, it reached No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 — the biggest pop hit of the Impressions' career.
It topped the R&B chart and sold a million copies, earning the group a gold record.
Cash later recalled that the song bought each of the three singers a house — by their early twenties, all three had homes and Cadillacs.
The lineup here is the classic trio: Mayfield, Fred Cash and Sam Gooden, after original lead Jerry Butler had gone solo.
Arranger Johnny Pate gave Mayfield's songs their lush, modern soul frame — the partnership modernized the group's sound in Chicago.
It anchored the group's self-titled debut album, released the same year.
Mayfield's falsetto-and-guitar style on records like this became a blueprint for soul music's next decade.
Huey Lewis & the News revived it in the 1990s, and a Jon Batiste–Celeste version carried it into Pixar's Soul (2020) for a new generation of kids.
The Impressions were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1991, with this song at the heart of their case.

title: Walking on Sunshine
description: Kimberley Rew wrote it, Katrina Leskanich sang it under a grey London sky, and the 1985 horn-driven remake became the most unstoppable good-mood song of the decade — pure joy with a backbeat.

pops.text: Guitarist Kimberley Rew wrote it; before the Waves, he'd played in the Soft Boys alongside Robyn Hitchcock.
The band first recorded it in 1983 for a Canada-only debut album — the version the world knows is the 1985 remake, rebuilt with punchy horns.
The remake was a worldwide hit in 1985: No. 9 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 8 in the UK.
Singer Katrina Leskanich is American, raised partly on US military bases, fronting a band formed in Cambridge, England.
The video plays the joke perfectly: London is grey and drizzling while Katrina, in summer clothes, bounces through it utterly unbothered.
Rew also wrote 'Going Down to Liverpool,' which the Bangles covered — the attention helped the Waves land their major-label deal.
The song became an advertising and movie-trailer evergreen, licensing its sunshine to decades of commercials.
Royalties from this one song reportedly kept the band comfortable for years — few three-minute investments have paid off better.
The Waves later won the 1997 Eurovision Song Contest for the UK with 'Love Shine a Light,' ending Britain's long Eurovision drought.
Leskanich has said she never tires of singing it — four decades on, audiences still start bouncing before the first chorus lands.

title: Stairway to Heaven
description: Eight minutes that build from John Paul Jones's recorder to one of rock's most famous solos — the Led Zeppelin IV centerpiece the band refused to release as a single, which only made it bigger.

pops.text: It closes the first side of Led Zeppelin IV (1971) and runs about eight minutes — an epic hiding on an untitled album with no band name on the cover.
Jimmy Page composed the music in sections; Robert Plant wrote most of the lyrics in one sitting at Headley Grange, the band's decaying country-house studio.
Atlantic Records wanted it as a single. Page and manager Peter Grant refused — fans would have to buy the whole album. They did.
The delicate opening is Page fingerpicking an acoustic guitar, with John Paul Jones playing recorders — Renaissance-fair instrumentation on a hard-rock record.
The famous guitar solo was played not on Page's usual Les Paul but on a Fender Telecaster, cut at Island Studios in London.
Through the 1970s it became the most-requested song on American FM rock radio, despite never being a chart single for the band.
Its sheet music became one of the best-selling pieces of sheet music in rock history — guitar shops everywhere learned to dread hearing it.
Claims that the song hides backwards Satanic messages sparked a 1982 California legislative hearing; the band always dismissed the idea.
In 2012, Heart's Ann and Nancy Wilson performed it at the Kennedy Center Honors, leaving Page, Plant and Jones visibly moved in the balcony.
A 2016 Los Angeles jury, after a high-profile copyright trial over the opening figure, found that 'Stairway' did not copy Spirit's 'Taurus.'
